Weights and Measures
WAYTS and MEZH-ers
noun phrase (theology / ethics)
From weight (Old English gewiht) and measure (Latin mensura); the standards of honest trade, which Scripture makes a matter of righteousness before God.

Biblical Definition

Weights and measures — the stones and balances and ephahs by which the ancient world bought and sold — are made by Scripture a matter of righteousness, not mere commerce, for the man who falsifies them robs his neighbor and offends his God. The merchant of old carried weights in his bag and measures in his shop; to keep two sets, a heavy stone for buying and a light one for selling, a large measure to receive and a small to give, was a common and hidden fraud. The law forbade it: "Thou shalt not have in thy bag divers weights, a great and a small... But thou shalt have a perfect and just weight, a perfect and just measure shalt thou have" (Deut 25:13–15). And the proverb states the principle as God's own concern: "A false balance is abomination to the LORD: but a just weight is his delight" (Prov 11:1); "Divers weights, and divers measures, both of them are alike abomination to the LORD" (Prov 20:10). The prophets thundered against the merchants who made the ephah small and the shekel great and falsified the balances by deceit (Amos 8:5). This dictionary confesses that honest weights and measures are a matter of the heart's integrity before God: the God who sees the scales in the dark delights in the just weight and abhors the false, and true religion shows itself in the marketplace as much as in the sanctuary.

Webster 1828 Definition

The standards of honest trade — balances, weights, and measures — which Scripture makes a matter of righteousness before God. The law forbids the double weight and false balance (Deut 25:13–15); a just weight is the LORD's delight and a false balance His abomination (Prov 11:1; 20:10).

WEIGHTS AND MEASURES, noun phrase. The standards of honest trade, made by Scripture a matter of righteousness.

The law forbids divers weights and measures — a great for buying, a small for selling (Deut 25:13–15).

"A false balance is abomination to the LORD: but a just weight is his delight" (Prov 11:1).

"Divers weights, and divers measures... are alike abomination to the LORD" (Prov 20:10).

The prophets condemned merchants who falsified the balances by deceit (Amos 8:5).

Key Scripture

Prov 11:1 — "A false balance is abomination to the LORD: but a just weight is his delight."

Deut 25:15 — "But thou shalt have a perfect and just weight, a perfect and just measure shalt thou have: that thy days may be lengthened in the land which the LORD thy God giveth thee."

Prov 20:10 — "Divers weights, and divers measures, both of them are alike abomination to the LORD."

Amos 8:5 — "making the ephah small, and the shekel great, and falsifying the balances by deceit."

Modern Corruption

The fraud of false weights never died; it only changed its instruments — the hidden fee, the misleading label, the rigged contract, the deceptive measure — and a privatized morality that imagines God indifferent to business dealings forgets that the LORD Himself weighs the scales and abhors the false balance.

expand to see more

The corruption is as old as trade and as new as the latest deception: the double weight, the false balance, the small ephah and the great shekel (Amos 8:5). The instruments change — the hidden charge, the doctored measure, the fine print framed to deceive, the contract written to rob — but the sin is one: defrauding the neighbor in the marketplace while keeping a respectable face. Scripture lifts this out of mere commerce and sets it before God: a false balance is His abomination (Prov 11:1).

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition, but a privatized morality imagines that religion belongs to the heart and the sanctuary while business runs by its own rules. Scripture knows no such division. The God who delights in a just weight (Prov 11:1) sees the scales in the dark shop, and He ties honest measures to His blessing in the land (Deut 25:15). The principle to recover is the integration of faith and trade: true religion is honest in the marketplace, and the just weight is the LORD's delight.
